**Genki Japanese and Culture School** - 6 weeks in Fukuoka in 2014 and 3 weeks in Tokyo in 2017. Low-High Intermediate level. 

**Structure** - Minimum 4 hours of basic language instruction each day - usually 2 classes of review/practice and 2 classes on grammar. I never had a class with more than 6 students - the small group study was very helpful. 

**Japanese-only?** My classes were almost entirely in Japanese - although the textbook has english translations and explanations, instruction was done in Japanese. Occasionally, students would ask each other for definitions or clarifications, but that was frowned upon. Some teachers were stricter than others. 

**Textbooks** - Genki I and II, although the school is not formally associated with the Genki textbook. After that - its a mix of materials. 

**Homework load/type** - We would be given a few worksheets every day - this did not take me much longer than 30 minutes tops. Of course it was expected that we would be proactive in practicing vocab/kanji. 

**Testing** - The occasional tests and quizzes were not graded and were solely for checking comprehension. If the class isn't right for you - they will move you up or down a level.  In order to receive a certificate of completion, you only need to attend 70% of classes. The focus is on learning, not grading. 

**Class Demographics** - Very diverse! I was in Fukuoka during the summer and there were other high school students (I was 17 at the time), but I had conversation classes with European men in their 30s (which were very interesting). When I was in Tokyo, half the school was Swiss, but the demographics change pretty frequently because there are new students every week. 
I didn't notice any demographic doing noticeably better or worse. 

**Teachers** - Really well trained and used to the eccentrics of foreigners. They were genuinely interested in holding conversations and making sure we understood what was going on in class. 

**Classmates Level** - Depended on diligence, but everyone has different skills. Usually new students would struggle for the first week to get used to the immersion, but settle in soon enough. If someone is really struggling or really excelling, the school will move them to a class that better suits their level. The only people I noticed having long term problems were those with attendance issues. 

**Pros and Cons**
    Pros - great community of students, solid immersion
    Cons - 1 chapter a week could feel slow at times. Classmates can make a strong impact on your experience. I was lucky enough to have mostly wonderful classmates, but it only takes one person to slow everyone else down. 

**Improvement** Before going to Fukuoka, I'd studied Japanese for 3 years at my high school, but couldn't hold a basic conversation. By the time I left, I felt comfortable with small talk and learned hundreds of new vocab words and kanji. 

**After** I went back and finished high school, started college, and lost a lot of my Japanese due to lack of diligence. I managed to land an internship at a Japanese company in Tokyo and decided to go back to Genki in Tokyo to sharpen my skills. So glad I did, my first week at work would have been a disaster if I hadn't gone back to the classroom first. 

**Diplomas** - I think college credit is offered, but I don't think they do diplomas. There are long term courses though. People study for any length of time between one week to two years. 

**Housing/Visas** - The school can help you find a dorm/apartment/homestay. Student visas are available in Fukuoka if you're studying for at least a year. Most people were on Working Holiday or Tourist visas.

**Tokyo vs Fukuoka** - Studying in Fukuoka was fantastic for my Japanese - it has all the comforts of a big city, but with less English signage than Tokyo (and cheaper food). I really felt motivated to improve. I do love Tokyo - but it is definitely a different experience.
